projectDesc.p: Encoded for the Experiencing War web site for the Veterans History Project.

samplingDecl.p: The recording of the interview with Fred Breger was digitized.

editorialDecl.p: This transcription was encoded with minimal changes to the original text in an effort to preserve original content and idiosyncrasies of the person interviewed. Period language and terminology are also retained. Encoding is literal with regard to the transcriptionist's capitalization, punctuation, and spelling. Spelling errors are indicated with [sic]; however, recurring errors in spelling within a single document have been marked the first time and not subsequently.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: This is the oral history of World War II veteran, Fred J. Breger. Mr. Breger served with the U. S. Navy. He served in the Pacific theater and was awarded the distinguished flying cross and an air medal with two clusters. I'm Tom Sworp (ph.) and we recording this at Mr. Bob Miller's home in Willoughby, Ohio. Bob's veteran's history was sent in on an earlier tape. We recorded this on May 21st, 2001, on a screened-in porch during a rain storm and that's the noise you hear in the background. Fred's age at the time of this recording was 77.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I was in the Navy from 1943 to '46, honorable discharge.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Had to get that in. I -- I started off at boot camp in Great Lakes and I went to Chicago -- No, I stayed at Navy Pier in Chicago for training as an aviation machinist's mate. Left there -- I'll probably get this screwed up a little bit but I'll try it. Left there and went to Oklahoma, I think. No. No. Went to Memphis and studied radar -- radar, then went to gunnery school in Yellow Water, Florida. Joined the squadron in Seattle, in Seattle, Washington, and after about a month there, we went up north to Arlington, Washington, joined a squadron. Two squadrons were at the base of Arlington and then went overseas from there.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: And went to -- to --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Which squadron would that be?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: There was a -- we had F4F fighters and TBF torpedo bombers, and we wound up in Washington for I would guess quite a number of months before we came down to Sandi -- Santa Anna and were there for a short time and then we got aboard a ship and went to Hawaii. And our -- our ship was docked right above the Arizona. They tell me you could see the tops of the stacks but I never did. The water may have been too cloudy. And from there, we -- we left there, I don't know when, sometime or '44 and went to our first battle was Luzon and then we went to Sumick (ph.) Bay and then we hid out someplace. No, we went first -- First, we went to Memmis (ph.) Island which is just north of Australia. And then we went up to Luzon and Sumick Bay. From there, we went to Iwo Jima, I think, and then Okinawa and then we came back --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: -- and roughly a year at sea.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: We came back and left -- We came back in at -- in San Diego and we went to Oklahoma, just kind of a cool-down thing and they shipped us back to Florida and we were in Florida for -- until separation time that separated in Toledo, 1946.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. So what was your rank?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: AMMC second class, Aviation Machinist's Mate second class, but I didn't do any of that work out there. I was an aerial gunner on a TBF.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: The upper gunner and two radio men down below and then me up above.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. And any particular vivid -- particularly vivid memories that you remember from overseas?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: One of the things that -- that surprised me -- I don't know if it's a good memory or bad -- but we would start our dives when we would drop bombs at about 10,000 feet and we'd pull out at about 700 feet. And what surprised me how you can feel your cheeks gettin' all -- all out of shape from -- from pulling out of the dives, you know, the G forces. We lost one ship that first -- first time we went down, down the Luzon, over a mountain, down and down the bridge and came up the other side of another mountain and one of our crew -- one of our crews got shot down by rifle fire off the side of the mountain. And the other things, we -- we were out in the ocean someplace, I can't tell you where, but the ships changed positions. We were submarine -- MS submarine patrols and the ships would change position every couple of hours. And we changed position with another ship, I think it was the Petrof Bay, but I'm not sure. Ours was Steamer Bay, CVE-87. And the Japanese hit us and they crashed a plane into the lower or the -- the rear elevator on -- on Petrof Bay and the back of the ship looked like just that last sheet metal on the back plus the -- the deck behind it with the six-inch gun just shot across the rudder about a half a mile standing straight up and then it went down. We were in that position an hour earlier, so we were saved by that hour.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What ship is that?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Steamer Bay.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Steamer Bay?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Petrof Bay got hit. I think it was the Petrof Bay. Of course, now I can't remember what I had for breakfast so --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Were you flying or _____?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Oh, yeah, we flew around Iwo. In fact, I -- I didn't know, you know, in the back, you had no idea how high you are. And so we were flying in a circle over -- not Iowa, Okinawa, and there was a big tank right by the main city there on the lower end which I don't remember the name of anymore, but they had one of these big gas tanks like Easter Island has, you know --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: -- fifty feet across and all that sort of stuff, so I thought, well, let's see if I can blow it up. So I aimed at it and I watched my projectiles. They hit down this -- down the road this side of the machine -- of the tank, and it -- there was a Japanese truck running along the road, just caught up to it and blew up the truck. That's the only thing I did worthwhile.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is that the only thing you remember hitting?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You didn't hit any subs, huh?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: No, I shot at a whale off Long Island someplace, which I felt bad about afterwards. I missed him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Thought it was a sub?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: No, I knew it was a whale.

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: During the ______

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: But I tried ______. What was your home town during the war?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Cleveland.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Cleveland?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Yeah. I grew up in Cleveland on 124th Street, moved to 125th when I was just born --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: -- stayed there 'til after the war. And the only really memorable thing I had -- I --I just read this happened to somebody else, there is a new -- a little paper out called the Escort Sailer's Magazine of some sort. Maybe you've heard of it. It's -- it's like a tabloid sheet --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: -- and somebody else had the same experience. We'd landed on the plane after a -- an allied submarine hop and they pulled us up in front of the island, last -- last plane in this parking deck, and I was still up in the -- in the turret and a fighter came in and he missed all three cables and he caught the -- caught the fence. They have I think three cables high. He caught that, flew up in the air, and as I got out of the -- of the plane, he landed right where I was sitting, head first, you know, the whole engine right there in the -- in the cockpit ... And that was interesting.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: And -- and North China Sea, I'll never forget this was the roughest bit of water we were ever in, and the ship pitched so hard to the side that I think we had four planes just rolled off the side. They broke their tie-down lines and fell off the side.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Did you enlist or were you drafted?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I was drafted. First -- first draft in Cleveland into the Navy.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Then they told me I might have to go into the Marines but -- if they needed me, so I didn't know from nothing, so I didn't care.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: But I didn't have to. And now that I know Mike went in, I'm glad I didn't. _____________________________________

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular memories of buddies or anything ___?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I do have a memory of, in fact, I didn't think our ship -- our crew, which was a pilot, radio man and myself, we were never close. I read all this stuff about, you know, you're -- you're cemented. This wasn't the case. And I -- I did have a good friend, Dee Gibson Hubbard, he was from Oklahoma, a really nice guy. He stayed -- He didn't stay in the service but he ended up stayed with flying and he became a -- a pilot for these oil rigs that go out in the ocean.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Of course, he's dead a few years back now. Really a -- a joyful guy. But, no, other than that, I didn't have any really close buddies.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is that by choice --

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Yes.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- you didn't want to get close?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: No. Just didn't happen. Just didn't happen ... Well, you know, I wasn't a drinker. I never swore as a kid. So, you didn't -- I didn't fit in with most of them. Okay. It's your turn to ask questions. I'm burned out.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Medals?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Yeah. I got a distinguished flying cross, three air medals, a couple of other ones but I wouldn't know ___ ___.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: And what would be the specific reason that they were awarded?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: It's written up on the -- on the paper but I don't remember.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You don't remember specifics?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I got them, that's all.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Well --

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I still -- I mean, I still have them. But I don't remember. I don't. Probably just for the campaign we were in, probably Luzon --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: No, that wasn't the biggest one, though. The biggest one was Okinawa, I think, and Iwo, of course. Mike was -- Bob just gave me a book to read. In fact, have you got it back yet?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: That -- that book that about the -- the Marines on Iwo Jima.

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: Oh, yeah, Flags of Our Fathers.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Yeah. Did you give it back yet? My brother asked me about it all the time.

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: No, I -- I -- I gave it to somebody else to read that was in church. He had it for a month. I don't know.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Oh, you promised to me -- to me -- That's -- that's why you don't have buddies. ______________________________________

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: They're turning that into a movie, too. I just read --

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Oh, really.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: -- yeah, someplace --

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I thought that was a terrific book.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh, I didn't read it, but I --

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: So I -- That book I did -- I didn't realize what the --

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: ________ Marine did, yeah.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I didn't realize what the Marines had to go through 'til I read that; I really didn't.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: _____ the author talking about it, his dad was one of the guys that raised the flag, right?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Now I got rid of him.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any -- backtracking a little bit -- any specific memories of Pearl Harbor Day?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Uhm, no. I was still home -- at home at -- at that time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That time --

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: No, that was '41. I graduated in June of '41, so I was six ahead of that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: No, I was just working in a factory and I never thought I'd ever get to the point of being in.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I didn't. I don't know, you know. As a kid, you think you know everything but you find out you don't.

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: _____ I was saying that --

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I had -- I had a girlfriend, so I wasn't really interested in going into the service.

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: Anyway, the _______ and I gave it to you when you were recuperating from the heart attack. When you asked me --

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Should I turn this around?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: No. No, you can go ahead.

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: -- if I ever had to stop and wipe my eyes while I was reading the book, and I said, "yes", then ___ might and say, "Hey, did you ever have to wipe your eyes or crying when you was reading the book?" And he said, "no".

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Yeah, I did, too.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I really was touched by that book.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you have any particular memories of letters from home, anything like that? Mail call?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I -- I -- I got a goodly selection of letters from home. Nothing special.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: They were all special but I mean nothing that stands out amongst all of them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I didn't save any of them.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Of course, when you're on -- on board a big E flight top, you got about that big of locker space. You don't save a heck of a lot.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: No, that -- that was the nice thing. The -- the place where we slept, our barracks as you'd call them I guess floated underneath the floor of the hanger -- the deck, the flight deck, and it -- it had those big holes in them, in the -- in the structural beam that went across. They -- they were the light in the beam and which we were in there one day watching a -- one evening watching a movie that they -- they made specially for the people home about carriers. Of course, they took the big one, and it was showing how the -- this -- this particular thing, I never forgot. They showed how they put the bombs on a little cart and they rolled them on a little bitty elevator just bigger than the cart and they take them up to the plane. And we didn't have anything like that. And so, after the movie was over, we went to -- went to bed, and we were in the North China Sea, and it was rough, and we heard this boom, crash, boom, crash, and we looked down through these big holes and there was a pound bomb down there rolling around the flight -- the hanger deck. It was crushing everything in -- everything in sight.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: And the next morning when we -- It didn't go off. Of course, they can't. But in the morning, the sides of the ship had bulges where that thing hit. That -- that -- that side couldn't have been more than five-sixteenths of an inch big.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: We had, you know, these little things like they would take the soldiers out to the shoreline, you know, and had that little gate in front that went down.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: And it had a big round bell on the top and they were out next to us and that little round bar hit the side of our ship and poked a hole in it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh ___.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Yeah. Yeah, another thing that happened there is to go from the hanger deck up, there was a stairway went up to a platform then went up to the hanger deck, and on that platform, there was a drinking fountain. And I don't -- I don't know, maybe it was one of our ships or -- or one of the Japanese ___, 'cause we -- we didn't come in contact with the ship ___, but -- but there was a lot of lead flying around. And from what they tell me, a 16-inch shell came through one side of the ship and out the other and took the drinking fountain and the guy taking a drink with him. And -- and, you know, it was just went [sound] as it went through the metal 'cause it was so thin. It was one of those Kaiser -- Kaiser-built carriers.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I guess that's another thing that happened on -- aboardship that we -- that we saw that movie I was just telling you about and then the day before they painted the boom, that's in front of the island, and they had this stuck out at a 45 degree angle so that the paint would dry. And while we were watching this movie, we heard a clunk, and went out in the morning, and there was a Japanese plane came right down that thing and the boom went right through the engine, right through the 13-year-old girl flying it and out the back end and she was hung up on that thing. Gee, now that hasn't come back to my memory for a long time.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Yeah, this -- this -- actually came right directly on it. Probably through the sun or the engine?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: And nobody even knew she was there until morning. Well, of course, the upper deck people did because they saw it.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: That's about it, I guess.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember when they dropped the bomb, where were you? The first one?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I think we were back in the states. I believe we were back in the states. And we were all surprised. We never heard of any program like that going on. We were happy they dropped it on Japan. No, other than that, I don't -- I think we were back. Do you remember what date they came down?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: That would be the second week of August, I believe, '45?

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: It was --

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I don't remember when we came back. I remember being out there when Easter Island gas fire happened 'cause we heard about that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Which island was that _____?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: I think so, yeah, then we came back. We were supposed to be back for a year and then go out on another tour.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Didn't happen.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Do you remember anything about celebrations on VE or VJ Day?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Yeah, VJ day, I was Oklahoma City. It was amazing. People were running all over kissing everybody under the sun. I think I could have got married 16 times that day. It was -- It was really fun. And Oklahoma was a dry city. I didn't drink but all the guys were going behind the hotel and coming out with bottles of hooch. Yeah, we hit -- we had a -- We were in Norman, Oklahoma, so we had to take a street car or an electric trolley of some sort into Oklahoma City. And it -- it was really just like you see on New Year's Eve downtown --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: -- and all that stuff. People all over. It was -- was really nice.

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: It must have been nice ... I said that it must have been nice.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: It was.

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: Nice celebration.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Any particular trouble adjusting to civilian life after the war?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: No, I don't think so. It was difficult getting back into different type of clothes after wearing a uniform. You know, that Navy uniform is tight but then it was open. Then you had to start wearing a tie and that sort of stuff, that was -- wasn't good. Oh, it took a while because when I -- when I got out, I -- I looked for a specific job and it paid very poorly. So, and in fact I -- I earned 50 bucks a month for the first couple of years. And that didn't go very far. Even then, it didn't. But no, I -- I think I adjusted fairly easily.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Did you go back to your prewar job then?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: No. No. Previously, I had -- I had worked in a machine shop and I didn't -- I found the -- the people in there dis -- not disliked. They -- they were just rotten talking about their whole families and I couldn't take that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: So I -- I went into architectural drafting and I got a job with a guy that had -- had a good -- Now, he's probably 70 years old. And I had difficulty finding a job. Everybody would look at you, say, "You should have been here during the war". And I was ?flip bird? -- I was just ready to -- to poke this guy through a window when -- when he told me that. If I'd have been here, where would he be? I found that was difficult getting -- getting a job. But once I start, I had no problem.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: It worked out fine.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Is anything else come to mind as a particularly vivid memory of your war time experience?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: No, not really ... No, I don't think so.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Oh, I have to tell you about the -- the one -- What's that thing you got for getting shot?

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: Purple Heart?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: One Purple Heart we had aboard the ship. We had more but only this one. The landing signal officer was on the back. And this one plane came in too close and he had to jump into a canvas sack and he had a -- a bottle of cough medicine in his back pocket. It broke and cut his butt, so he got the distinguished flying cross.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: What do you think about the guys that were -- that landed into China and gettin' medals? Yeah, I'll tell you I think we're medal happy, this country.

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: He was just discussing that.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: _____ remember they --

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: Oh, yeah, they gave out more medals there. Eight thousand troop I thought ___ I thought I read. ______________________________________________________

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: And 16,000 medals.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: You talking about the combat infantryman ten hours out there ______________.

sp.speaker: Unidentified voice
sp.p: Ninety days before I gotten my __________________ --

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: Uh-huh. Anything else?

sp.speaker: Fred Breger
sp.p: Not that I can think of.

sp.speaker: Tom Swope
sp.p: All right.
[CONCLUSION OF INTERVIEW; END OF SIDE ONE, TAPE ONE]
